usage: existence takes 가, never 를: 기회가 있다
잡다 (grab) is the default verb, not 하다
좋은 modifies the noun directly, no 의
set phrase for a soft, open-ended offer
examples: 기회가 있어요?
Is there a chance?
simplest existence frame with 가 있다
저는 외국에서 일할 기회를 잡고 싶어요.
I want to seize a chance to work abroad.
a verb + ㄹ 기회 = 'a chance to do X'
좋은 기회였는데 그때 안 잡아서 지금도 아쉬워요.
It was a good opportunity, but I didn't take it then, so I still regret it.
real-talk: 기회를 잡다/놓치다 in past reflection
nuance: 기회 (機會, 機 'opportune moment/device' + 會 'meeting') is a window of opportunity that may not come twice, so it carries a faint pressure to act. The key contrast is 기회 vs 기능: 기회 is a chance to do something, while 기능 is a 'function/feature.' Koreans treat 기회 as something you physically handle — 기회를 잡다 (seize), 기회를 놓치다 (miss), 기회를 주다/얻다 (give/get) — so the partner verb is concrete, never 기회를 하다. With existence it is 기회가 있다/없다, and 기회가 되면 is a gentle, non-committal 'if the chance comes up.' The English-speaker trap is twofold: don't say 기회를 하다 by mapping 'take a chance' word-for-word, and don't mark existence with 를 (기회를 있다 ✗ → 기회가 있다 ✓). Register is neutral, fine in both polite speech and writing.

usage: describing state takes 가, not 를
신랄한 평가; can sound like a complaint
examples: 태도가 좋아요.
Your attitude is good.
simple praise; state-adjective with 가
그분은 일에 대한 태도가 정말 진지해요.
That person's attitude toward work is really serious.
에 대한 태도 = the standard 'attitude toward X' frame
실수한 뒤에 태도를 싹 바꿔서 다들 놀랐어요.
After the mistake he completely changed his attitude, so everyone was surprised.
real-situation: 태도를 바꾸다 + adverb 싹 (cleanly/completely)
nuance: 태도 (態度, 態 'state/manner' + 度 'degree') is the disposition someone reveals through behavior — their stance toward work, people, or a situation. Contrast it sharply with 자세: 자세 can be a literal body posture ('sit up straight' = 자세를 바로 하다) and a metaphorical mindset, but 태도 stays in the mental/behavioral lane and never means physical posture. Habitual collocations are 일에 대한 태도, 태도가 좋다/나쁘다, 태도를 바꾸다, 진지한/적극적인 태도. Note the social weight: 태도가 나쁘다 about a person is a real criticism, so use it carefully with superiors. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'have a good attitude' tempts 태도를 좋다 ✗ — but 좋다 is descriptive, so it must be 태도가 좋다 ✓ (를 only with action verbs like 바꾸다).

usage: descriptive adjective takes 이, not 을
확인하다 = verify; common in work email
examples: 내용이 어려워요.
The content is hard.
simplest state sentence with 이
회의 내용을 간단히 정리해서 보냈어요.
I summarized the meeting content briefly and sent it.
내용을 정리하다 — staple office collocation
문자 내용이랑 실제 약속 시간이 달라서 다시 확인했어요.
The text's content and the actual appointment time differed, so I checked again.
real-situation: 내용 = the substance/wording inside a message
nuance: 내용 (內容, 內 'inside' + 容 'contain') is the substance or gist inside something — a book, message, lecture, contract — as opposed to its outer form. The sharp contrast is 내용 (what it says) vs 형식 (the form/format): a report can have weak 내용 but proper 형식. Don't confuse it with a physical container either; the box itself is 상자/봉투, while 내용물 specifically means the physical 'contents' (items) inside a package. Typical partners: 내용을 이해하다/정리하다/확인하다, 내용이 어렵다/풍부하다, 회의 내용, 문자 내용. The English-speaker pitfall is particle choice driven by the adjective: 'the content is hard' becomes 내용이 어렵다 ✓, not 내용을 어렵다 ✗ — 를/을 attaches only to action verbs like 이해하다, never to descriptive 어렵다.

usage: quantity adjective takes 가, not 를
needs 의 before the noun it classifies
같은 종류의 X = 'the same type of X'
examples: 종류가 많아요.
There are many kinds.
simplest frame; 많다 takes 가
어떤 종류의 음악을 좋아하세요?
What kind of music do you like?
어떤 종류의 + noun — the 의 is required
같은 종류의 제품인데 매장마다 가격이 달라요.
They're the same kind of product, but the price differs from store to store.
real-situation: 같은 종류의 for classifying, not counting
nuance: 종류 (種類, 種 'seed/kind' + 類 'category') is the type or category something belongs to, so 종류가 많다 means 'there are many varieties.' The crucial contrast is 종류 vs 가지: 종류 classifies by KIND (어떤 종류의 음악 'what kind of music'), whereas 가지 is a counter for tallying items (세 가지 방법 'three methods'). They overlap loosely in speech, but 종류 cannot replace 가지 as a number-counter, and 가지 cannot ask 'what type.' Habitual partners: 종류가 많다/다양하다, 어떤 종류, 같은/다른 종류, 여러 종류. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: 'there are many kinds' tempts 종류를 많다 ✗ → 종류가 많다 ✓ (많다 is descriptive); and learners drop the linking 의 — 'what kind of music' is 어떤 종류의 음악, not 어떤 종류 음악 ✗.

usage: noun + 수준 compounds with no particle
examples: 수준이 높아요.
The level is high.
state-adjective 높다 with 이
제 한국어 수준은 아직 중급이에요.
My Korean level is still intermediate.
noun + 수준: 한국어 수준, no 의 needed
꾸준히 연습해서 실력 수준을 한 단계 높이고 싶어요.
I want to raise my skill level up one notch by practicing steadily.
real-situation: 수준 (overall level) + 단계 (a discrete step)
nuance: 수준 (水準) literally composes 水 'water' + 準 'level' — picture a carpenter's water level, hence an abstract gauge of where ability or quality sits. It measures how HIGH/LOW something is: 수준이 높다/낮다, 수준을 높이다, 생활 수준, 한국어 수준. The sharp contrast is 수준 vs 단계: 수준 is a continuous level on a scale ('the class is high-level'), while 단계 is a discrete step/stage in a sequence ('move to the next stage' = 다음 단계로). You raise your 수준 but advance through 단계. Note a social caution: saying someone's 수준이 낮다 sounds dismissive about their class/quality, so it can land as an insult. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle — 'the level is high' is 수준이 높다 ✓, not 수준을 높다 ✗; 을 appears only with the action verb 높이다 (raise).

Confusing 수준 (a level on a scale) with 단계 (a discrete step/stage in a sequence)

examples: 상태가 좋아요.
The condition is good.
simplest state sentence with 가
요즘 잠을 못 자서 건강 상태가 안 좋아요.
I haven't slept well lately, so my health condition isn't good.
건강 상태 + 안 좋다 (negated state)
중고차라서 사기 전에 상태를 꼼꼼히 확인했어요.
Since it's a used car, I checked its condition carefully before buying.
real-situation: 상태를 확인하다 about a physical object
nuance: 상태 (狀態, 狀 'shape/form' + 態 'condition') is the present condition of one specific thing — a person's health, an object, a system — captured at a moment. The sharp contrast is 상태 vs 상황: 상태 zooms in on the CONDITION of a single entity (건강 상태 'health condition'), while 상황 is the broader CIRCUMSTANCE/situation surrounding events (교통 상황 'traffic situation', 지금 상황이 복잡해요). Habitual partners: 상태가 좋다/나쁘다, 상태를 확인하다, 건강/배터리/도로 상태, ~한 상태 ('in a … state'). A handy grammar use: 술에 취한 상태로 = 'in a drunken state.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'the condition is good' is 상태가 좋다 ✓ (좋다 descriptive), never 상태를 좋다 ✗; and don't reach for 상황 when you mean one thing's condition.

Forgetting the compound has no particle: it is 건강 상태, not 건강의 상태 in everyday speech

usage: a verb + 는 모습 = 'the image of doing'
examples: 모습이 보여요.
I can see the figure.
보이다 'be visible' takes 이, intransitive
오랜만에 친구의 밝은 모습을 봐서 기뻤어요.
I was glad to see my friend looking cheerful after so long.
모습을 보다 — here you actively look (보다, takes 를)
열심히 일하는 부모님의 모습이 아직도 눈에 선해요.
The image of my hardworking parents is still vivid in my mind's eye.
real-situation: ~하는 모습 + 눈에 선하다 (vividly remembered)
nuance: 모습 is a native Korean word (고유어, not Sino-Korean) for the visible figure, look, or scene of a person or thing — and crucially the whole impression of how someone appears or behaves, e.g. 일하는 모습 'the sight of someone working.' The sharp contrast is 모습 vs 얼굴: 얼굴 is just the face, whereas 모습 takes in the entire silhouette, manner, and even a remembered image. It also differs from 외모, which is narrowly 'physical looks/attractiveness'; 모습 is more about the captured sight or impression, often with emotional warmth. Watch the transitivity pair: with 보이다 (be visible) use 모습이 보이다 (intransitive, 이); with 보다 (look at) use 모습을 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing these — 모습을 보이다 ✗ for 'something is visible'; that should be 모습이 보이다 ✓ (모습을 보이다 instead means 'to show a certain side of oneself').

examples: 분위기가 좋아요.
The atmosphere is nice.
simplest vibe sentence with 가
이 카페는 분위기가 정말 편안해서 자주 와요.
This cafe has a really relaxing atmosphere, so I come often.
분위기가 편안하다 — describing a place's vibe
회식 분위기가 가라앉아서 제가 농담으로 분위기를 띄웠어요.
The company-dinner mood sank, so I lifted it with a joke.
real-situation: 분위기가 가라앉다 vs 분위기를 띄우다 (passive sink / active lift)
nuance: 분위기 (雰圍氣, 雰 'mist/vapor' + 圍 'surround' + 氣 'air/energy') is literally 'the air that surrounds you' — the collective mood of a place, gathering, or moment. The sharp contrast is 분위기 vs 기분: 분위기 is the SHARED vibe in the room (회식 분위기가 좋다), while 기분 is one person's INNER feeling (제 기분이 좋다 'I'm in a good mood'). Mixing them is the classic error: 'I'm in a good mood' is 기분이 좋아요, not 분위기가 좋아요 (which describes the room, not you). The English-speaker pitfall, beyond 기분 confusion, is the particle: 분위기를 좋다 ✗ → 분위기가 좋다 ✓.

examples: 시험 범위가 넓어요.
The exam scope is wide.
시험 범위 + 넓다 (descriptive, 가)
예산 범위 안에서 가구를 골랐어요.
I chose furniture within the budget range.
범위 안에서 = 'within the bounds of'
발표 주제의 범위를 조금 줄이는 게 좋겠어요.

real-situation: 범위를 줄이다/정하다 — actively set bounds
nuance: 범위 (範圍, 範 'pattern/model' + 圍 'enclose') is the bounded extent something covers — an exam syllabus, a budget, a topic. It is measured 넓다/좁다 (wide/narrow): 범위가 넓다, 시험 범위, 예산 범위, 범위 안에서. The sharp contrast is 범위 (the SPAN/extent covered) vs 한계 (the outer LIMIT you can't pass): 시험 범위가 넓다 means 'the exam covers a lot,' while 체력의 한계 means 'the ceiling of one's stamina.' Don't confuse 범위 with 사이 either — 사이 is the gap or relationship between two specific points/people. 범위 leans formal and written, common in study and work. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'the range is wide' is 범위가 넓다 ✓, not 범위를 넓다 ✗ (넓다 is descriptive; 를 only with action verbs like 정하다/줄이다).

範圍 = 範 'pattern/model' + 圍 'enclose' — the enclosed area within set bounds.
The particle is the trap: 'the range is wide' is 범위가 넓다 ✓, not 범위를 넓다 ✗ (넓다 is descriptive; 를 only with action verbs like 정하다/줄이다).

mistakes: Saying 범위를 넓다 ✗ — 넓다 is descriptive, so use 가: 범위가 넓다 ✓
Confusing 범위 (the span covered) with 한계 (the outer limit you cannot exceed)
Using 범위 for the space between two points/people — that is 사이 (둘 사이)

usage: noun + 의 + 한계 = 'the limit of X'
examples: 한계가 있어요.
There is a limit.
existence frame with 가 있다
혼자서 할 수 있는 일에는 한계가 있어요.
There's a limit to what I can do alone.
~에는 한계가 있다 = 'there's a limit to ~'
야근이 계속되니까 이제 체력의 한계를 느껴요.
Since the overtime keeps going, I now feel the limit of my stamina.
real-situation: 체력의 한계를 느끼다 — reaching one's ceiling
nuance: 한계 (限界, 限 'restrict' + 界 'boundary') is the outer ceiling beyond which something can't go — ability, stamina, patience. 한계를 느끼다 means 'to feel you've hit your limit,' and 한계를 넘다/극복하다 means to push past or overcome it. The sharp contrast is 한계 (the LIMIT you cannot exceed) vs 끝 (the plain END point of a thing): a road has an 끝, but human endurance has a 한계 — 끝 is concrete/sequential, 한계 is the abstract maximum. It also differs from 범위 (the SPAN covered, not the ceiling). Habitual partners: 한계가 있다, 한계를 느끼다/넘다/극복하다, 체력의/인내의 한계. The English-speaker pitfall is the existence particle: 'there is a limit' is 한계가 있다 ✓, not 한계를 있다 ✗ — existence always takes 가/이, never 를/을.
